Social Knowledge for Cross-Domain User Preference Modeling

Figure 1 · How much data is needed?

MAP rises quickly with the number of entities in the user representation and levels off beyond about 100 sampled accounts. With k = 50 sampled accounts, SE1 reaches 98.5% of its full-profile score (paper: 98.4%). In the closed world, 10 entities already give 99.0% of the full score.

2Notes on the original code

Things I found while matching the notebooks. None of them changes the paper's conclusions.

Bug

Target entities were never removed

The "All" profile subtracts screen names from a set of numeric ids, which removes nothing, so the target category stays in the profile. Removing it properly moves overall MAP from 0.571 to 0.567 (+22% → +21%).

Labels

Two classifier outputs are flipped

The socialvec package labels the age and education outputs backwards. Read as shipped, 98% of 60 Minutes followers would be under 25. The paper's figure, and this reproduction, use the corrected reading.

Sampling

SE1 samples can't be redrawn exactly

The original order came from a set of string ids, which changes with every Python run. Redrawn with the same seed, the overall values land within ±0.004. The closed-world (SE2) samples match exactly.

Detail

"Entities" are followed accounts

SE1 samples k followed accounts, and only about 43% of them are SocialVec entities. The paper's "1,972 entities per user" counts all followed accounts.

3Extension · Less popular entities

Does social user modeling still help when the candidates aren't the most famous entities in their category?

In the 9 categories that list 100 typed entities, I sorted the entities by Twitter follower count and ranked those at positions 81–100 instead of the top 20. No category lists more, so ranks 100–120 were not possible. User profiles exclude every listed entity of the target category. As a matched control, I ranked the original top 20 for the same users with the same profiles. A random ranking (exact expected AP) provides a chance level, and paired Wilcoxon tests compare the two methods.

  • Popularity breaks down in the tail. At ranks 81–100 it scores 0.298, barely above a random ranking (0.259), and below it for News outlets, Politicians, TV stations and Journalists.
  • Social similarity holds up. It scores 0.413, well above chance in every category, and beats popularity in 8 of 9 categories. Its relative gain grows from +22% on the top 20 to +39%.
  • The result holds on a population ten times larger. On all experiment users (36,739 user–category pairs), the gain is +38% vs. +24%, and every per-category difference is significant (p < 0.001).
  • The exception is Comedians (−26%). Follows in that band concentrate on its two most-followed accounts, both mainly political commentators, which popularity ranks first.

Limitations

Only the original top-20 candidates were manually validated; the lower ranks include some mistyped entities (esports teams among sports teams, party accounts among TV stations). Users were sampled as followers of the top-20 entities. Users follow only 1.4–5.6 band candidates each, so per-user AP is noisy in the smaller categories.

4Open items

Not run

GPT-4o experiment (Table 3)

The pipeline is ready and tested offline. It needs Azure OpenAI credentials and about 33.5K calls; a trial run on 5 users per category is available.

Next

Description-based tail candidates

The requested variant selects 50–100 accounts per category by their textual descriptions and requires them to be below the top 10K/20K SocialVec entities. My band used the existing typed lists and follower counts: 20 candidates per category, of which only 110 of 177 fall below the top 10K. The ranking protocol carries over unchanged.

Regenerate the underlying results with python run_reproduction.py and python run_popularity_band.py --start 81 --end 100. Details are in results/REPORT.md and results/POPULARITY_BAND_REPORT.md.
